q: A 64-year-old is listed for off-pump CABG. Compared with on-pump CABG, which is the main anaesthetic advantage of the off-pump technique?
o: No risk of conversion to bypass
why: Avoiding CPB reduces the systemic inflammatory response and coagulopathy, with less re-exploration and ventilator/ITU time (any POCD/stroke benefit is theoretical; trials show no difference at 5 years). Haemodynamic instability from handling the heart is the main disadvantage, and about 10% convert to CPB.

q: During off-pump grafting of the circumflex artery the heart is lifted into a stabiliser. BP falls from 120/70 to 65/35 mmHg and the ECG shows new ST depression. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Tell the surgeon and ask for the heart to be repositioned while supporting the BP
Ask the perfusionist to go on bypass immediately
why: Positioning and immobilisation devices reduce filling. Close communication with the surgeon is a core goal: release or reposition the heart while supporting the MAP (target above 70 mmHg). Conversion to CPB is the escalation if this fails.

q: Which is the target mean arterial pressure during off-pump coronary grafting?
o: Within 10% of the pre-induction value only
why: The goal is a MAP above 70 mmHg to maintain coronary perfusion while vessels are occluded, with pacing wires available for bradycardia and active warming.

q: Before induction a patient’s cerebral oximetry (NIRS) baseline is 74%. During surgery it falls to 55%. What should you do first?
o: Check for artefact: reposition the probe and check the headband is not too tight
why: A fall of more than 20% from baseline is significant. Exclude artefact first, then optimise oxygen delivery (Hb, MAP above 65, FiO2, PaCO2 4.5–5.5 kPa) and oxygen consumption (depth of anaesthesia, seizures).

q: Which statement about near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) cerebral oximetry is correct?
o: It needs pulsatile flow to give a reading
It uses light at around 760 and 850 nm and the Beer–Lambert law
A 10% fall from baseline is significant
It measures jugular venous oxygen saturation
why: NIRS uses near-infrared light (around 760 and 850 nm) and the Beer–Lambert law. It does not need pulsatile flow, so it works on bypass. Baseline is typically around 60–75% and changes are judged against the patient’s own baseline; a fall of more than 20% is significant.

q: In pre-operative assessment, climbing two flights of stairs without stopping corresponds to roughly how many METs?
why: Two flights without stopping is the usual practical marker of at least 4 METs (Miller’s table puts one flight at about 5 METs and gardening at 4). Self-report is unreliable, so a structured tool such as DASI is preferred. 1 MET = 3.5 ml O2/kg/min.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of Lee’s Revised Cardiac Risk Index?
why: The six RCRI factors are ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, raised creatinine and high-risk surgery. Age is not included.

q: Four hours after CABG, a patient’s chest drain output suddenly stops. BP is falling, CVP is rising and heart sounds are quiet. A PA catheter is in place. Which finding most supports the likely diagnosis?
o: Equalisation of diastolic pressures across the chambers
A large v wave on the PCWP trace
High cardiac output with low SVR
Falling pulmonary artery pressures with rising CVP
why: This is tamponade (Beck’s triad: low BP, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds). A PA catheter shows equalised diastolic pressures; echo shows chamber collapse and a dilated IVC.

q: You are inducing anaesthesia for re-sternotomy for cardiac tamponade. Which haemodynamic goal is most important?
o: Allow a slow heart rate to improve filling time
Reduce SVR to improve forward flow
Keep the patient “fast, full and tight”, avoiding bradycardia
Use positive pressure with high PEEP before the chest is opened
Give a large dose of propofol to blunt the pressor response
why: Stroke volume is fixed and limited, so cardiac output depends on heart rate. Maintain preload, rate, SVR and contractility, avoid bradycardia, and have the surgeon scrubbed before induction.

q: A patient in cardiac ICU after cardiac surgery develops VF. A defibrillator is attached immediately. What is the recommended first step?
o: Start external chest compressions and give adrenaline 1 mg
Deliver up to three stacked shocks
Open the chest immediately for internal massage
why: After cardiac surgery, VF/pVT is treated with three stacked shocks first. Then give early amiodarone 300 mg, FiO2 1.0, remove PEEP, avoid full-dose adrenaline and aim to re-open within 5 minutes if needed.
